stem: A team's CLAUDE.md has grown to include a 40-step production deploy checklist that is used once a week. It costs context in every session, and the team never wants Claude to start a deploy on its own. Which change best fits?

options.text: Move the checklist into a rule file under .claude/rules/ without path frontmatter.
options.explanation: A rule without paths loads at launch just like CLAUDE.md, so it would still cost context in every session.

options.text: Move it into a skill with disable-model-invocation set to true.
options.explanation: Correct. A skill's body loads only when used, and disabling model invocation ensures only a person can trigger the deploy.

options.text: Move it into a separate file and import it from CLAUDE.md with an @path reference.
options.explanation: Imported files load at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them, so the context cost doesn't change.

options.text: Delete it and rely on auto memory to recall the procedure.
options.explanation: Auto memory is machine-local notes Claude writes itself. It's neither a reliable procedure nor a control on who can deploy.

stem: Earlier in a session, a developer and Claude agreed that log timestamps are in UTC. Claude then delegated log analysis to a custom subagent, which reported times as local time and drew the wrong conclusion. Why did this happen, and what fixes it?

options.text: The subagent lacks a memory field, so add one and it will read the main conversation's history.
options.explanation: A memory field gives a subagent its own persistent notes, not access to the parent conversation.

options.text: The context window was full, so the developer should run /compact before delegating again.
options.explanation: Compaction affects the main conversation only. The subagent would still start without that decision.

options.text: Subagents can't read CLAUDE.md, so the UTC rule has to be written into the subagent's model setting.
options.explanation: The model field chooses a model. It isn't a place for instructions, and the issue is missing context from the conversation.

options.text: Subagents run in their own context window, so the delegation prompt must include the UTC decision.
options.explanation: Correct. A subagent starts with its own context and returns only its result. Anything decided in the main conversation has to be passed along explicitly.

stem: A CI job runs `claude -p "run the tests and fix failures"`. Every Bash call is denied, and the job ends without running the tests. The author assumed it would behave like their interactive sessions, which start in auto mode. Which fix best fits?

options.text: Pre-approve the test command with --allowedTools, since -p runs start in Manual mode.
options.explanation: Correct. Non-interactive runs start in default (Manual) mode, where calls needing approval are denied unless something approves them.

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md line telling Claude that it has permission to run shell commands in CI.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is guidance, not permission. It can't approve a tool call that the permission system denies.

options.text: Run the job with bypassPermissions on the shared CI runner so nothing is ever denied.
options.explanation: Bypass is meant for isolated containers or VMs only, and it skips all safety checks. A narrow allowlist meets the need.

options.text: Switch the job to an interactive session so a CI operator can approve each prompt as it appears.
options.explanation: CI has nobody to answer prompts. Headless runs are designed to be configured up front.

stem: An open-source project wants a CI job that runs `claude -p` to triage pull requests from external forks. Any fork could add its own `.claude/settings.json` hooks or `.mcp.json` servers. Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Rely on Claude Code's workspace trust dialog to block hooks and MCP servers from untrusted folders.
options.explanation: A -p run shows no workspace trust dialog, so the project's hooks and MCP servers would load without one.

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude to ignore any hooks or servers that the fork defines.
options.explanation: Hooks and MCP servers are loaded by the client, not chosen by the model. An instruction can't stop them, and the fork controls that file too.

options.text: Run with --bare, pass the triage instructions in the prompt, and limit tools with --allowedTools.
options.explanation: Correct. --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md, so fork-supplied configuration never loads.

options.text: Run with --dangerously-skip-permissions inside the CI container so the job never blocks on prompts.
options.explanation: Skipping permissions removes checks rather than adding them. The fork's hooks and servers would still load.

stem: Halfway through a long debugging session, a developer's context is nearly full, but they want to keep working on the same bug. Later they'll switch to an unrelated documentation task. Which TWO commands fit these two needs? (Select TWO.)

options.text: /compact with a focus hint, to summarize the bug session and keep going.
options.explanation: Correct. /compact frees space by summarizing the current conversation, so the bug work continues with its key details.

options.text: /rewind, to permanently delete the oldest messages and free up space.
options.explanation: /rewind rolls the conversation or code back to a checkpoint. It isn't a way to keep going with less context.

options.text: /clear, to start an empty conversation for the documentation task.
options.explanation: Correct. /clear starts fresh for unrelated work, and the old conversation stays resumable.

options.text: /init, to regenerate CLAUDE.md so the session context is reset.
options.explanation: /init drafts or improves a project CLAUDE.md. It doesn't manage the conversation's context.

options.text: /context, to compress the conversation into a shorter summary.
options.explanation: /context shows what's using the context window. It doesn't change it.

stem: A release script runs Claude Code headless to list functions that are missing docstrings, then feeds the list to another program. The downstream parser breaks whenever the output format varies. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Use the default text output and ask Claude in the prompt to answer only with a JSON array.
options.explanation: A prompt request is not a guarantee, and text output gives no schema check. The parser would still break occasionally.

options.text: Use --output-format stream-json and concatenate all the text deltas into one string.
options.explanation: Streaming events help with real-time display. Reassembling them gives the same unvalidated text.

options.text: Add --bare so that no CLAUDE.md content can change the shape of the answer.
options.explanation: --bare speeds startup and skips auto-discovery, but it doesn't constrain the output format.

options.text: Use --output-format json with --json-schema and read the structured_output field.
options.explanation: Correct. With a JSON Schema, the result arrives in structured_output in a shape the parser can rely on.

stem: An analyst named a Claude Code session `draft-board` while working on mock-draft logic yesterday. Since then she has run several other sessions in the same directory, and now wants to pick up the draft-board work where it left off. Which command best fits?

options.text: claude --continue, which reopens the most recent conversation in this directory.
options.explanation: --continue picks the most recent conversation, which is now one of her later sessions, not draft-board.

options.text: claude, then paste in a summary of yesterday's work.
options.explanation: A pasted summary loses detail and wastes effort when the full conversation can be resumed.

options.text: claude --resume draft-board, which resumes that session by name.
options.explanation: Correct. --resume takes a session ID or name, so it reopens exactly the conversation she wants.

options.text: claude --fork-session, which opens a copy of yesterday's most recent session.
options.explanation: --fork-session only works together with --resume or --continue, and on its own it doesn't choose the right session.

stem: A developer on a company laptop is tired of approving every file edit and test run, and proposes starting Claude Code with `bypassPermissions`. The security team insists that risky actions such as force-pushes still be checked. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Use bypassPermissions, but add a CLAUDE.md note asking Claude to be careful with git.
options.explanation: Bypass is only for isolated containers or VMs, and a CLAUDE.md note doesn't enforce anything.

options.text: Use auto mode, where a classifier reviews actions and blocks risky ones, and keep deny rules for pushes.
options.explanation: Correct. Auto mode removes most prompts while a separate classifier checks each action, and deny rules still apply in every mode.

options.text: Use dontAsk mode so that anything that would normally prompt runs automatically.
options.explanation: dontAsk does the opposite: anything not pre-approved is denied. It suits locked-down CI, not interactive work.

options.text: Use plan mode, which approves edits and commands once the plan has been accepted.
options.explanation: Plan mode is for exploring and proposing changes before editing. It isn't designed to remove prompts during implementation.

stem: A team wants two things from Claude Code. SQL migration conventions should load only when Claude works on files under `db/migrations/`. An investigator should explore the codebase with read-only tools without flooding the main conversation. Which TWO mechanisms best fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a migrations section to the root CLAUDE.md so the conventions are always available.
options.explanation: Root CLAUDE.md loads in every session, so the conventions would cost context even when nobody touches migrations.

options.text: A rule in .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter matching db/migrations/**.
options.explanation: Correct. A path-scoped rule loads only when Claude works on matching files, which is exactly the condition the team gave.

options.text: Import the conventions file into CLAUDE.md with an @path reference to keep it separate.
options.explanation: Imports organize content but load at launch, so the conventions would still be in context all the time.

options.text: Ask Claude to save the conventions to auto memory the first time someone edits a migration.
options.explanation: Auto memory is machine-local and loaded each session. It doesn't scope content to a path or share it with the team.

options.text: A subagent in .claude/agents/ whose tools field lists only read-only tools such as Read, Grep and Glob.
options.explanation: Correct. A subagent runs in its own context window and returns only a summary, and restricting its tools keeps it read-only.

stem: A developer opens Claude Code for the first time in an existing scouting-database repository. They want every future session to know the build and test commands and the team's naming conventions, with as little manual writing as possible. Which first step best fits?

options.text: Run `/compact` at the end of each session so the conventions carry over to the next one
options.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the current conversation. It does not carry knowledge into new sessions, which each start with a fresh context window.

options.text: Run `/init` to draft a CLAUDE.md from the codebase, then trim it to the facts every session needs
options.explanation: Correct. `/init` drafts the project CLAUDE.md, which loads at the start of every session. Trimming it keeps the per-session context cost low.

options.text: Write the commands and conventions into a skill so they load only when someone types its name
options.explanation: Facts needed in every session belong in CLAUDE.md. A skill's body loads only when invoked, so Claude would not know the build commands otherwise.

options.text: Explain the conventions in chat once and rely on the conversation history for later sessions
options.explanation: A new session does not see earlier conversations. Chat-only explanations have to be repeated every time.

stem: Over several weeks, a developer corrected Claude Code about how the team names play-by-play fixture files, and Claude now gets it right on their laptop. A colleague who cloned the same repository gets the old, wrong naming. What explains this, and which fix best fits?

options.text: The colleague's model is older; pinning the same model in both users' settings will share the learned behaviour
options.explanation: Model choice doesn't explain it. The learned rule lives in memory files, not in the model.

options.text: The colleague has auto memory disabled; turning it on with `/memory` will sync the developer's notes to them
options.explanation: Turning on auto memory starts the colleague's own local notes. It does not copy another machine's memory.

options.text: Auto memory is stored per machine under `~/.claude/`; put the naming rule in the committed project CLAUDE.md
options.explanation: Correct. Auto memory is machine-local, so the corrections never left the developer's laptop. A team-wide convention belongs in the project CLAUDE.md, which is committed and shared.

options.text: The colleague must resume the developer's old sessions with `claude --resume` to inherit the corrections
options.explanation: Sessions are local too, and resuming a conversation is not a sharing mechanism for conventions.

stem: Twenty minutes into a refactor of a depth-chart module, a developer realises Claude has been heading in the wrong direction: several files were edited and the conversation is full of reasoning built on a bad assumption. They want both the code and the conversation back to how they were before the refactor began. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Run `/clear` to start an empty conversation and continue from there
options.explanation: `/clear` starts a fresh conversation but leaves the edited files as they are.

options.text: Run `git checkout .` and keep going in the same conversation
options.explanation: This restores the files but leaves the bad assumption in the conversation, so Claude is likely to repeat it.

options.text: Run `/compact` with a note that the earlier approach was wrong
options.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation; it doesn't undo file edits, and the summary may still carry the bad reasoning.

options.text: Run `/rewind` and restore both the code and the conversation to the checkpoint before the refactor
options.explanation: Correct. `/rewind` can roll back the conversation, the code or both to an earlier checkpoint, which is exactly the stated need.

stem: A league's IT team manages all developer laptops. Policy says no developer may use Claude Code's auto mode, and Claude must never run `rm -rf` in any permission mode. Individual developers must not be able to override either rule. Which TWO measures best fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add "never use auto mode and never run rm -rf" to every repository's CLAUDE.md
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is guidance Claude reads, not enforcement, and it doesn't stop a developer from choosing auto mode.

options.text: Set `disableAutoMode` in managed settings
options.explanation: Correct. Managed settings sit above user and project settings and can't be overridden, and this key removes auto mode.

options.text: Ask developers to start Claude Code with `bypassPermissions` so prompts never interrupt the policy
options.explanation: Bypass mode removes approval prompts altogether, which weakens control rather than enforcing the policy.

options.text: Put a deny rule for the command in each developer's user settings file
options.explanation: A user-level file is under the developer's control, so the rule can be removed. The policy needs a level developers can't change.

options.text: Add a deny rule for `Bash(rm -rf *)` in managed settings
options.explanation: Correct. Deny rules apply in every permission mode, including bypass, and placing the rule in managed settings stops developers from removing it.

stem: A team's `/scout-report` skill runs a long procedure: it reads dozens of files and produces a one-page summary. Every time it runs, the main conversation fills with the intermediate file reads, and later work in the session suffers. Which change best fits?

options.text: Move the procedure into CLAUDE.md so it is always loaded and needs fewer reads
options.explanation: This adds context to every session and doesn't stop the file reads landing in the conversation.

options.text: Set `context: fork` in the skill's frontmatter to run it in a forked context
options.explanation: Correct. A forked context keeps the skill's intermediate work out of the main conversation, which receives only the result.

options.text: Run `/clear` after each report so the file reads are removed
options.explanation: This also throws away everything else in the session that the developer still needs.

options.text: Set `disable-model-invocation: true` so the skill uses less context
options.explanation: That setting controls who can trigger the skill, not where its work happens.

stem: Early in a Claude Code session, before much work has been done, a developer notices that the context is already well filled. They want to see what is taking up the space, such as CLAUDE.md, MCP tools or skills, before deciding what to trim. Which command best fits?

options.text: `/context`, which shows what is using the window
options.explanation: Correct. `/context` breaks down what is occupying the window, so the developer can see what to trim.

options.text: `/compact`, which summarizes the conversation so far
options.explanation: Compacting summarizes the conversation without showing what was using the space, and the startup load would remain.

options.text: `/init`, which regenerates the project's CLAUDE.md
options.explanation: `/init` drafts or improves CLAUDE.md. It doesn't report context usage.

options.text: `/rewind`, which restores an earlier checkpoint
options.explanation: Rewinding rolls back the conversation or code. It doesn't show what fills the window.
